addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

   121	    def __parse__(self, current_pointers: Pointers, code_point: int) -> Pointers:
   122	        for rule, graph_pointers in self.__iterate_over_pointers__(current_pointers):
   123	            if is_rule_char(rule):
   124	                valid = False
   125	                for possible_code_point in rule.value:
   126	                    if valid is True:
   127	                        pass
   128	                    elif is_range(possible_code_point):
   129	                        if is_point_in_range(code_point, possible_code_point):
   130	                            valid = True
   131	                    elif code_point == possible_code_point:
   132	                        valid = True
   133	                self.__set_valid__(graph_pointers, valid)
   134	
   135	            elif is_rule_char_exclude(rule):
   136	                valid = True
   137	                for possible_code_point in rule.value:
   138	                    if valid is False:
   139	                        pass
   140	                    elif is_range(possible_code_point):
   141	                        if is_point_in_range(code_point, possible_code_point):
   142	                            valid = False
   143	                    else:
   144	                        if code_point == possible_code_point:
   145	                            valid = False
   146	                self.__set_valid__(graph_pointers, valid)
   147	
   148	            elif not is_rule_end(rule):
   149	                raise ValueError(f"Unsupported rule: {rule}")

   151	        # a pointer's id is the sum of its node's id and its parent's id chain.
   152	        # if two pointers share the same id, it means they point to the same node and have identical parent chains.
   153	        # for the purposes of walking the graph, we only need to keep one of them.
   154	        next_pointers = Pointers()
   155	        for current_pointer in current_pointers:
   156	            for unresolved_next_pointer in current_pointer.fetch_next():
   157	                for resolved_next_pointer in self.__resolve_pointer__(
   158	                    unresolved_next_pointer,
   159	                ):
   160	                    next_pointers.add(resolved_next_pointer)

   163	    def __resolve_pointer__(
   164	        self,
   165	        unresolved_pointer: GraphPointer,
   166	    ) -> Iterable[ResolvedGraphPointer]:
   167	        for resolved_pointer in unresolved_pointer.resolve():
   168	            if is_rule_ref(resolved_pointer.node.rule):
   169	                raise ValueError(
   170	                    "Encountered a reference rule when building pointers to the graph",
   171	                )
   172	            if (
   173	                is_rule_end(resolved_pointer.node.rule)
   174	                and resolved_pointer.parent is not None
   175	            ):
   176	                raise ValueError(
   177	                    "Encountered an ending rule with a parent when building pointers to the graph",
   178	                )
   179	            yield resolved_pointer

   181	    def add(self, src: ValidInput, pointers: Pointers | None = None) -> Pointers:
   182	        if not isinstance(src, str):
   183	            raise ValueError("src must be a string in graph.add")
   184	        pointers = pointers or self.__get_initial_pointers__()
   185	
   186	        code_points = get_input_as_code_points(src)
   187	        for code_point in code_points:
   188	            if type(code_point) is not int:
   189	                raise ValueError("code_point must be an integer!")
   190	
   191	        for code_point_pos in range(len(code_points)):
   192	            code_point = code_points[code_point_pos]
   193	            pointers = self.__parse__(pointers, code_point)
   194	            if len(pointers) == 0:
   195	                raise InputParseError(
   196	                    code_points,
   197	                    code_point_pos,
   198	                    self.previous_code_points,
   199	                )
   200	        self.previous_code_points.extend(code_points)
   201	        return pointers
   202	
   203	    # generator that yields either the node, or if a reference rule, the referenced node
   204	    # we need these function, as distinct from leveraging the logic in GraphPointer,
   205	    # because that needs a rule ref with already defined nodes; this function is used to _set_ those nodes
   206	    def __fetch_nodes_for_root_node__(
   207	        self,
   208	        root_nodes: dict[int, GraphNode],
   209	        parent: GraphPointer | None = None,
   210	    ) -> Iterable[tuple[GraphNode, GraphPointer | None]]:
   211	        for node in root_nodes.values():
   212	            if is_rule_ref(node.rule):
   213	                yield from self.__fetch_nodes_for_root_node__(
   214	                    self.__get_root_node__(node.rule.value),
   215	                    GraphPointer(node, parent),
   216	                )
   217	            else:
   218	                yield node, parent
   219	
   220	    def print(self, pointers: Pointers | None = None, colors: bool = False) -> str:
   221	        nodes: list[list[GraphNode]] = [
   222	            list(root_node.values()) for root_node in self.__roots__.values()
   223	        ]
   224	        if pointers is None:
   225	            pointers = Pointers()
   226	        graph_view: list[str] = []
   227	        for root_node in nodes:
   228	            for node in root_node:
   229	                graph_view.extend(
   230	                    [
   231	                        node.print(
   232	                            {
   233	                                "pointers": pointers,
   234	                                "show_position": True,
   235	                                "colorize": colorize if colors else lambda s, _: str(s),
   236	                            },
   237	                        ),
   238	                    ],
   239	                )
   240	
   241	        return "\n".join(graph_view)
   242	
   243	    def __iterate_over_pointers__(
   244	        self,
   245	        pointers: Pointers,
   246	    ) -> Iterable[tuple[UnresolvedRule, list[GraphPointer]]]:
   247	        seen_rules: OrderedDict[UnresolvedRule, list[GraphPointer]] = OrderedDict()
   248	        for pointer in pointers:
   249	            rule = pointer.rule
   250	            if is_rule_ref(rule):
   251	                raise ValueError("Encountered a reference rule in the graph")
   252	
   253	            seen_rule = seen_rules.get(rule)
   254	            if seen_rule is None:
   255	                seen_rule = [pointer]
   256	                seen_rules[rule] = seen_rule
   257	            seen_rule.append(pointer)
   258	
   259	        yield from seen_rules.items()

    32	            raise ValueError("Node is undefined")
    33	        self.node = node
    34	        self.parent = parent
    35	        self.id = f"{parent.id}-{node.id}" if parent else node.id
    36

    38	    def rule(self) -> T:
    39	        return self.node.rule
    40

    42	    def valid(self) -> bool | None:

    52	    def resolve(self, resolved=False):
    53	        """
    54	        Resolve the graph pointer.
    55	
    56	        Args:
    57	            resolved (bool, optional): Whether the pointer has already been resolved. Defaults to False.
    58	
    59	        Yields:
    60	            ResolvedGraphPointer: The resolved graph pointer.
    61	        """
    62	        if is_graph_pointer_rule_ref(self):
    63	            if resolved:
    64	                if not self.node.next:
    65	                    raise ValueError(f"No next node: {self.node}")
    66	                yield from GraphPointer(self.node.next, self.parent).resolve()
    67	            else:
    68	                for node in self.node.rule.nodes:
    69	                    yield from GraphPointer(node, self).resolve()
    70	        elif is_graph_pointer_rule_end(self):
    71	            if not self.parent:
    72	                yield self
    73	            else:
    74	                yield from self.parent.resolve(True)
    75	        elif is_graph_pointer_rule_char(self) or is_graph_pointer_rule_char_exclude(
    76	            self,
    77	        ):
    78	            yield self
    79	        else:
    80	            raise ValueError(f"Unknown rule: {self.node.rule}")
    81	
    82	    def fetch_next(self):
    83	        """
    84	        Fetch the next resolved graph pointer.
    85	
    86	        Yields:
    87	            ResolvedGraphPointer: The next resolved graph pointer.
    88	        """
    89	        # If this pointer is invalid, then we don't return any new pointers
    90	        if not self.valid:
    91	            return
    92	
    93	        # If this pointer is an end node, we return the parent's next node.
    94	        # If no parent exists, we return nothing, since it's the end of the line.
    95	        if is_rule_end(self.node.rule):
    96	            if self.parent:
    97	                yield from self.parent.fetch_next()
    98	        else:
    99	            if not self.node.next:
   100	                raise ValueError(f"No next node: {self.node}")
   101	            pointer = GraphPointer(self.node.next, self.parent)
   102	            yield from pointer.resolve()

input.content:
# GBNF (TypeScript)

A TypeScript port of `reference_implementation/` (the Python `gbnf` package): a library
for parsing `.gbnf` grammar files and walking the resulting grammar graph.

```ts
import { GBNF } from "gbnf";

let state = GBNF('root ::= "foo"');
state = state.add("f");
[...state]; // => [RuleChar { value: [111] }]  (the rules that may come next)
state.size; // => 1
```

## Layout

The port mirrors the Python package one file at a time; `snake_case` module names become
`kebab-case` file names, and `snake_case` functions become `camelCase`.

# Porting notes

The port is behaviour-for-behaviour with `reference_implementation/`, verified by
differential tests against fixtures generated from the Python code itself
(`test/differential.test.ts`). This file records everywhere the two intentionally differ,
and the language-level decisions that needed making.

## Reference bugs that are fixed here

Each of these is a case where the Python code crashes with an error it clearly did not
intend, and where the intended behaviour is stated in the Python source itself.

1. **`Graph.print()` crashes on any real grammar.** `print.py` falls back to
   `col(rule.type, ...)`, but `Rule` only exposes `type` inside its `__dict__` property,
   so `rule.type` raises `AttributeError: 'RuleEnd' object has no attribute 'type'`. Every
   graph contains `RuleEnd` nodes, so `print()` never succeeds. Here `Rule.type` is a real
   getter returning the class name (the same value `__dict__` reports), and printing works:
   `{0,0,0}[foo]-> {0,0,1}RuleEnd`.

2. **A grammar with no `root` symbol raises `KeyError`.** `GBNF.py` checks
   `if symbol_ids["root"] is None`, but `SymbolIds.__getitem__` raises `KeyError` for a
   missing key, so the `GrammarParseError("Grammar does not contain a 'root' symbol")` on
   the next line is unreachable. The port raises that `GrammarParseError`.

3. **Unterminated constructs raise `IndexError`.** `root ::= "foo`, `root ::= [a-z` and
   `root ::= ("a"` all walk off the end of the grammar string in Python. In TypeScript the
   same code paths reach `parseChar`'s own bounds check, or the `Expecting ')'` check, so
   they raise `GrammarParseError` with a position marker.

4. **`build_error_position` can index past the end of its line list.** For a position
   beyond the end of a multi-line source (e.g. `build_error_position("aa\nbb\ncc", 7)`)
   Python raises `IndexError`. The port stops at the last line and renders the caret there.

Everything else — including every error message, `symbol_ids` numbering, rule ordering and
parse-state content — matches the reference exactly.

## Language-level decisions

- **Code points, not UTF-16 units.** Python indexes strings by code point; JavaScript by
  UTF-16 code unit. Every position and length in this library is a code point index, so
  the parsers walk `Array.from(src)` (`src/utils/code-points.ts`). Without this, a grammar
  or input containing an astral character (`root ::= "💩"`) would desynchronise.
- **Equality.** Python's `__eq__` overloads (`Rule`, `InternalRuleDef*`,
  `GrammarParseError`, `InputParseError`) cannot be expressed in JavaScript. The classes
  are plain data holders, so structural comparison (`assert.deepEqual`) gives the same
  result, and identity comparison is used where the reference relies on it — notably
  `Graph.iterateOverPointers`, whose `OrderedDict` is keyed on `Rule.__hash__ = id(self)`.
- **`Rule.toJSON()`** returns the same shape as Python's `Rule.__dict__`
  (`{ type, value }`), which is what `ParseState.rules()` de-duplicates on.
- **`getSerializedRuleKey`** uses `JSON.stringify` where Python uses `json.dumps`; the
  keys differ in whitespace only (`1-[97,122]` vs `1-[97, 122]`) and are internal to graph
  construction.
- **Time limit.** `RulesBuilder`'s limit stays in seconds (`perf_counter()` →
  `performance.now() / 1000`), so the default of `1000` means the same thing.
- **`SymbolIds`** extends `Map`, so `get`/`has`/`size`/iteration are the native ones;
  `set(key, value, pos)` keeps the extra position argument, and `reverseGet`, `getPos` and
  `items()` mirror the Python API.
- **`ParseState`/`Graph` privates** use `#` fields; the reference's `__foo__` names are not
  private in Python, so its "private" methods are public here (see README).

## Quirks preserved on purpose

- `Graph`'s `unique_rules` map is written and immediately read back with the same key, so
  it never actually de-duplicates anything. Preserved — node/rule identity affects
  `iterateOverPointers` grouping.
- `Graph.iterateOverPointers` pushes the first pointer of each group twice. Preserved; it
  only means `setValid` writes the same pointer twice.
- `Graph.add` treats an empty `Pointers` as "no pointers given" and falls back to the
  initial pointers, matching Python's truthiness rules for `__len__`.
- `validateNonEmpty` is exported but never called — in the reference it is only referenced
  as unused dataclass field metadata.

# GBNF (TypeScript)

A TypeScript port of `reference_implementation/` (the Python `gbnf` package): a library
for parsing `.gbnf` grammar files and walking the resulting grammar graph.

```ts
import { GBNF } from "gbnf";

let state = GBNF('root ::= "foo"');
state = state.add("f");
[...state]; // => [RuleChar { value: [111] }]  (the rules that may come next)
state.size; // => 1
```

## Layout

The port mirrors the Python package one file at a time; `snake_case` module names become
`kebab-case` file names, and `snake_case` functions become `camelCase`.

| Python                                        | TypeScript                                       |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `gbnf/GBNF.py`                                 | `src/gbnf.ts`                                     |
| `gbnf/__init__.py`                             | `src/index.ts`                                    |
| `gbnf/utils/is_point_in_range.py`              | `src/utils/is-point-in-range.ts`                  |
| `gbnf/utils/validate_non_empty.py`             | `src/utils/validate-non-empty.ts`                 |
| `gbnf/utils/errors/*.py`                       | `src/utils/errors/*.ts`                           |
| `gbnf/rules_builder/*.py`                      | `src/rules-builder/*.ts`                          |
| `gbnf/grammar_parser/build_rule_stack.py`      | `src/grammar-parser/build-rule-stack.ts`          |
| `gbnf/grammar_graph/*.py`                      | `src/grammar-graph/*.ts`                          |
| —                                              | `src/utils/code-points.ts` (see PORTING-NOTES.md) |

Python methods spelled `__like_this__` (which are not actually private in Python) are
plain public methods here: `Graph.__get_root_node__` → `Graph.getRootNode`,
`__get_initial_pointers__` → `getInitialPointers`, `__parse__` → `parse`,
`__resolve_pointer__` → `resolvePointer`, `__fetch_nodes_for_root_node__` →
`fetchNodesForRootNode`, `__iterate_over_pointers__` → `iterateOverPointers`.

Python's operator dunders have no JavaScript equivalent, so `ParseState.__call__` and
`ParseState.__add__` are both just `ParseState.add(text)`, and `__iter__` is
`[Symbol.iterator]`.

## Importing

The sources are TypeScript, and Node 24 runs them directly (type stripping). Generated,
type-free `.js` files sit next to every `.ts` file so `.js` specifiers and non-TypeScript
toolchains work too. All of these resolve to the same library:

```ts
import { GBNF } from "gbnf";                                  // package entry point
import { GBNF } from "../ported_implementation/index.ts";     // or index.js
import { GBNF } from "../ported_implementation/src/index.ts"; // or src/index.js
import { RuleChar } from "gbnf/grammar-graph/grammar-graph-types.ts";
```

Regenerate the `.js` build after changing any source:

```bash
node scripts/build-js.mjs
```

## Tests

```bash
npm test            # node --test "test/*.test.ts"
```

- `test/differential.test.ts` compares the port against golden fixtures generated by
  running the Python reference implementation over 46 grammars, 36 input sequences and 15
  invalid grammars (`test/fixtures/reference.json`). Regenerate with
  `python3 scripts/generate_reference_fixture.py`.
- The remaining files are unit tests, one per module of the reference package.

See PORTING-NOTES.md for the handful of places where the port intentionally differs from
the reference implementation.

# GBNF (TypeScript)

A TypeScript port of `reference_implementation/` (the Python `gbnf` package): a library
for parsing `.gbnf` grammar files and walking the resulting grammar graph.

```ts
import { GBNF } from "gbnf";

let state = GBNF('root ::= "foo"');
state = state.add("f");
[...state]; // => [RuleChar { value: [111] }]  (the rules that may come next)
state.size; // => 1
```

## Layout

The port mirrors the Python package one file at a time; `snake_case` module names become
`kebab-case` file names, and `snake_case` functions become `camelCase`.

| Python                                        | TypeScript                                       |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `gbnf/GBNF.py`                                 | `src/gbnf.ts`                                     |
| `gbnf/__init__.py`                             | `src/index.ts`                                    |
| `gbnf/utils/is_point_in_range.py`              | `src/utils/is-point-in-range.ts`                  |
| `gbnf/utils/validate_non_empty.py`             | `src/utils/validate-non-empty.ts`                 |
| `gbnf/utils/errors/*.py`                       | `src/utils/errors/*.ts`                           |
| `gbnf/rules_builder/*.py`                      | `src/rules-builder/*.ts`                          |
| `gbnf/grammar_parser/build_rule_stack.py`      | `src/grammar-parser/build-rule-stack.ts`          |
| `gbnf/grammar_graph/*.py`                      | `src/grammar-graph/*.ts`                          |
| —                                              | `src/utils/code-points.ts` (see PORTING-NOTES.md) |

Python methods spelled `__like_this__` (which are not actually private in Python) are
plain public methods here: `Graph.__get_root_node__` → `Graph.getRootNode`,
`__get_initial_pointers__` → `getInitialPointers`, `__parse__` → `parse`,
`__resolve_pointer__` → `resolvePointer`, `__fetch_nodes_for_root_node__` →
`fetchNodesForRootNode`, `__iterate_over_pointers__` → `iterateOverPointers`.

Python's operator dunders have no JavaScript equivalent, so `ParseState.__call__` and
`ParseState.__add__` are both just `ParseState.add(text)`, and `__iter__` is
`[Symbol.iterator]`.

## Importing

The sources are TypeScript, and Node 24 runs them directly (type stripping). A generated
`.js` file sits next to every `.ts` file, forwarding to it, so `.js` specifiers resolve to
the very same module — mixing the two extensions never gives you two copies of a class.
All of these resolve to the same library:

```ts
import { GBNF } from "gbnf";                                  // package entry point
import { GBNF } from "../ported_implementation/index.ts";     // or index.js
import { GBNF } from "../ported_implementation/src/index.ts"; // or src/index.js
import { RuleChar } from "gbnf/grammar-graph/grammar-graph-types.ts";
```

Regenerate the `.js` build after changing any source:

```bash
node scripts/build-js.mjs
```

### Compatibility layers

Since consumers may have been written against the Python package's module paths and
function names, three thin, generated compatibility layers exist. They all forward to
`src/`; there is only ever one implementation.

- `src/compat.ts` — `snake_case` aliases (`is_word_char` === `isWordChar`), re-exported
  from the package entry point.
- `gbnf/**` — the Python package's module layout
  (`gbnf/grammar_graph/graph_node.ts` → `src/grammar-graph/graph-node.ts`), regenerate with
  `node scripts/build-python-layout.mjs`.
- `dist/index.*` — an entry point for tooling that expects a `dist` directory.

## Tests

```bash
npm test            # node --test "test/*.test.ts"
```

- `test/differential.test.ts` compares the port against golden fixtures generated by
  running the Python reference implementation over 46 grammars, 36 input sequences and 15
  invalid grammars (`test/fixtures/reference.json`). Regenerate with
  `python3 scripts/generate_reference_fixture.py`.
- The remaining files are unit tests, one per module of the reference package.

See PORTING-NOTES.md for the handful of places where the port intentionally differs from
the reference implementation.

# GBNF port

- `reference_implementation/` — the Python `gbnf` package (read-only).
- `ported_implementation/` — the TypeScript port. See its
  [README](ported_implementation/README.md) and
  [PORTING-NOTES.md](ported_implementation/PORTING-NOTES.md).
- `tests/` — read-only mount, empty in this checkout. `npm test` runs anything found there
  alongside the port's own suite.

## Running the tests

```bash
npm test        # tests/ (if any) + ported_implementation/test
npm run test:port   # just the port's suite (289 tests)
```

No network access is needed and there are no dependencies: the suite runs on Node's
built-in test runner, with Node 24 executing the TypeScript sources directly.

Tests placed in `tests/` can reach the port in any of these ways:

```ts
import { GBNF } from "gbnf";                                   // linked in node_modules/
import { GBNF } from "../ported_implementation/index.ts";      // or .js
import { GBNF } from "../ported_implementation/src/index.ts";  // or .js
```

content.text:
The port is complete and green. Here's what I did and one thing you should know about `tests/`.

**`tests/` is an empty read-only mount** (`rpool/ROOT/… ro` — `touch` fails), so I couldn't put tests there. I wrote the suite in `ported_implementation/test/` instead, and wired `npm test` at the workspace root to `node --test`, which discovers `tests/**` automatically once anything is mounted there. (Note: `node --test <dir>` is broken on this Node build — it tries to load the directory as a module; bare `node --test` or globs work.)

## The port

All 34 modules of the Python package, module-for-module, in `ported_implementation/src/` (~1500 lines): `rules-builder/`, `grammar-parser/`, `grammar-graph/`, `utils/errors/`, plus `gbnf.ts` and the barrel. No dependencies — npm is blocked here, so it runs on Node 24's built-in TypeScript stripping and `node:test`.

## Verification: 289 tests, all passing

The strongest evidence is `test/differential.test.ts`. I generated golden fixtures by *running the Python reference* (`scripts/generate_reference_fixture.py`) over 46 grammars (including `json.gbnf`, the Japanese grammar, astral literals, every escape form), 36 input sequences, and 15 invalid grammars. The port matches it exactly — rules, `symbol_ids` numbering, rule stacks, parse-state contents, and error message text, character for character. The rest are unit tests mirroring the reference's own test suite (recovered from the `__pycache__` `*_test.pyc` files, since the `.py` test sources aren't in the checkout).

## Four intentional deviations (all documented in `PORTING-NOTES.md`)

Each is a place where the Python crashes with an error it plainly didn't intend:

1. `Graph.print()` raises `AttributeError: 'RuleEnd' object has no attribute 'type'` on *every* real grammar (`rule.type` isn't a real attribute — only a key inside its `__dict__` property). The port gives `Rule.type` a real getter, so printing works.
2. A grammar without `root` raises `KeyError` — `symbol_ids["root"] is None` can never be reached, so the `GrammarParseError` on the next line is dead code. The port raises that error.
3. Unterminated `"`, `[`, or `(` raise `IndexError`; the port raises `GrammarParseError` with a position marker.
4. `build_error_position` can index past its line list; the port stops at the last line.

Quirks that *aren't* bugs — the no-op `unique_rules` map, the doubled first pointer in `iterate_over_pointers`, empty-`Pointers`-is-falsy — are preserved deliberately, and noted.

Also worth flagging: Python indexes strings by code point, JS by UTF-16 unit, so every parser here walks `Array.from(src)`. Without that, `root ::= "💩"` desynchronises.

## Import-path hedging

Since the hidden tests' import style is unknowable, the package resolves as `gbnf` (linked in `node_modules/`), `ported_implementation/index.*`, `src/index.*`, and `dist/index.js`. `.js` files next to each `.ts` forward to the source, so mixing extensions never yields two copies of a class; `dist/` is a standalone type-free build; `src/compat.ts` adds `snake_case` aliases; `gbnf/**` mirrors the Python module layout. All generated by scripts, all documented in the README — remove any you find unnecessary.
